tagline: The book of Israel's rescue from slavery in Egypt, the covenant God makes with them at Mount Sinai, and the tent where he comes to live among them.
overview:
Exodus begins with a family that has become a nation and a nation that has become a slave people. The seventy descendants of Jacob who went down to Egypt at the end of Genesis have multiplied, and a new Pharaoh, afraid of their numbers, puts them to forced labor and orders their baby boys drowned. God raises up Moses, a Hebrew child pulled from the Nile and raised in Pharaoh's household, calls him from a burning bush in the wilderness, and reveals his name. Through ten plagues God breaks Pharaoh's grip, and on the night of the Passover he brings Israel out. At the sea he destroys Pharaoh's army, and in the desert he feeds his people with manna and gives them water from the rock.

The second half of the book takes place almost entirely at Mount Sinai. There God makes a covenant (a binding, sworn relationship with obligations on both sides) with the people he has rescued, gives them the Ten Commandments and a body of laws, and gives detailed instructions for a portable sanctuary, the tabernacle, where he will dwell among them. Almost at once the people break the covenant by worshiping a golden calf. Moses intercedes, God renews the covenant and proclaims his own character, and the book ends with the tabernacle built and the glory of the LORD filling it.

Exodus is the Old Testament's central story of salvation. Psalmists, prophets, and apostles return to it again and again to explain what God is like and what it means to be rescued by him. Its movement is from slavery to worship. Israel is freed from serving Pharaoh in order to serve the LORD, and the story does not end on the far shore of the sea but on the day God comes to live with his people.
author:
Exodus, like the rest of the Pentateuch (the first five books of the Bible, called the Torah in Jewish tradition), does not name its author. Jewish and Christian tradition has long held that Moses wrote it, and the book itself says Moses wrote down particular material: the record against Amalek (17:14), the words of the LORD at the covenant ceremony (24:4), and the words of the renewed covenant (34:27). Jesus refers to the account of the burning bush as part of the book of Moses (Mark 12:26). Many conservative scholars hold that Moses is the substantial source of the book, while allowing for later editing such as the updating of place names.

Since the nineteenth century many critical scholars have instead seen the Pentateuch as woven together from several sources written over centuries. The classic form of that view, the Documentary Hypothesis associated with Julius Wellhausen, identified four sources (usually labeled J, E, D, and P) and dated the priestly material, which includes much of the tabernacle section, to the time of the Babylonian exile or after. Many scholars have since moved away from the neat four-source scheme toward other models, often distinguishing simply between priestly and non-priestly material, and the debate about how and when the book reached its final form continues. Readers across these views agree that Exodus as we have it is a carefully shaped whole.
date:
Two dates matter here: when the events happened and when the book was written. For the exodus itself, two main dates are proposed. The earlier date, around 1446 BC, comes from counting back from 1 Kings 6:1, which places the exodus 480 years before the fourth year of Solomon's reign (about 966 BC). The later date, in the thirteenth century BC and often under Ramesses II (who reigned about 1279 to 1213 BC), rests on the name of the store city Rameses in Exodus 1:11 and on the pattern of new village settlement in the hill country of Canaan around 1200 BC; its defenders read the 480 years as a round figure for twelve generations. The earliest mention of Israel outside the Bible, on the victory stela of Pharaoh Merneptah from around 1208 BC, names Israel as a people already living in Canaan. Some scholars doubt that the exodus happened as described, or think the escape of a smaller group grew into the story of the whole nation. No Egyptian record mentions the event, which defenders of its history note is unsurprising, since Egyptian royal inscriptions rarely if ever recorded defeats.

The date of writing follows from a reader's view of authorship: the time of Moses on the traditional view, and anywhere from the early monarchy to the Persian period (the fifth century BC) for the book's final form on various critical views.
setting:
Exodus opens in the eastern Nile Delta, the region Genesis calls Goshen, where Egypt met the land bridge to Canaan. Egypt was the great power of the age. Its king, the Pharaoh, was regarded as a son of the sun god and the earthly embodiment of the god Horus, and its wealth rested on the yearly flooding of the Nile and on vast building projects carried out by conscripted and foreign labor. The book never names the Pharaoh of the oppression or of the exodus; it calls him only by his title. Semitic peoples from Canaan are well attested in the Delta through the second millennium BC. A line of foreign rulers known as the Hyksos governed northern Egypt for about a century before being driven out around 1550 BC, and some scholars connect the new king who did not know Joseph with the suspicion of foreigners that followed.

After leaving Egypt, Israel moves through the wilderness of the Sinai Peninsula to the mountain of God, called both Sinai and Horeb. Its location is debated. Christian tradition since late antiquity has identified it with Jebel Musa in the southern peninsula, while others propose sites in the northern Sinai or in northwest Arabia, the region of Midian. The first readers were Israelites who needed to know who they were, where they had come from, and which God had claimed them, whether they first heard the book on the edge of the promised land, under the kings, or rebuilding after exile.
purpose: Exodus tells Israel who its God is and who they are because of what he has done. It explains the origin of the Passover, the Sabbath as a sign of the covenant, the priesthood, and the tabernacle, and it grounds Israel's law in a rescue. The Ten Commandments open with the words “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” Obedience is the response of a freed people, not the price of freedom. The book also warns, through the golden calf, how quickly a rescued people can make a god of its own, and it shows that Israel's survival depends on a God who forgives and still goes with them.
story: Exodus picks up where Genesis ends. Genesis closes with Jacob's family settled in Egypt and Joseph's dying promise that God would bring them up to the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Exodus shows the first part of God's promise to Abraham (a great nation) fulfilled even under oppression, and the rescue begins because God remembers his covenant with the patriarchs. The book ends with God dwelling in the tabernacle at Sinai, which leads straight into Leviticus, where God speaks from that tent and teaches a sinful people how to live near a holy God. Numbers then carries them from Sinai through forty years in the wilderness to the edge of Canaan. Across the rest of the Bible the exodus becomes the pattern for every later rescue. The prophets describe the return from Babylon as a new exodus (especially in Isaiah 40 to 55), and the New Testament describes the work of Jesus in its language.
christ: The New Testament reads the exodus as the pattern that Jesus fills. Jesus died at Passover, and at the Last Supper, a Passover meal, he spoke of the cup as his blood of the covenant, echoing the covenant blood Moses sprinkled on the people in Exodus 24:8. Paul calls Christ our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), and John notes that none of Jesus' bones were broken, recalling the rule for the Passover lamb in Exodus 12:46 (John 19:36). At the transfiguration, Luke says Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about his departure, using the Greek word exodos (Luke 9:31). John says the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, using a verb built on the word for a tent, and that his glory was seen, as the glory once filled the tabernacle (John 1:14). Jesus calls himself the true bread from heaven, greater than the manna (John 6), and his “I am” sayings in John's Gospel are widely read against the name revealed at the bush. Hebrews reads the tabernacle and its priesthood as copies and shadows of the heavenly reality that Christ has entered (Hebrews 8 to 10). Exodus itself does not name a Messiah; what it gives the church are the categories (redemption, the lamb, covenant blood, God dwelling among his people, glory) in which it learned to understand him.
reading:
Exodus combines several kinds of writing: narrative (chapters 1 to 19 and 32 to 34), law (chapters 20 to 23), and detailed instructions and building reports for the tabernacle (chapters 25 to 31 and 35 to 40). Readers often hurry through the tabernacle chapters, but their length is part of the point. The book gives as much space to God's dwelling as to Israel's rescue, and the building report largely repeats the instructions to show the people doing exactly what God said. Watch for repeated phrases: God hearing the cry of the oppressed, the refrain that Egypt and Israel will know that he is the LORD, and the verb serve, since the same Hebrew root describes slavery to Pharaoh and the worship of God.

A few misreadings are common. The laws are not a ladder by which Israel earned God's favor; they are given to people already rescued. The plagues are neither random natural disasters nor mere magic; the text presents them as judgments on the gods of Egypt (12:12). And the hardening of Pharaoh's heart should be read alongside the verses that say Pharaoh hardened his own heart. The large numbers in the book (600,000 men on foot in 12:37) are also debated. Some take them at face value, while others argue that the Hebrew word for thousand can also mean a clan or a military unit, which would make the company much smaller.

structure.title: Oppression in Egypt and the birth of Moses
structure.summary: Jacob's descendants multiply in Egypt, and a fearful Pharaoh enslaves them and orders their sons killed. Moses is saved from the Nile, raised by Pharaoh's daughter, and flees to Midian after killing an Egyptian. God hears Israel's cry.

structure.title: The call of Moses
structure.summary: God appears to Moses in a burning bush, reveals his name, and sends him to Pharaoh. Moses resists, Aaron is given as his spokesman, and the first demand to Pharaoh only makes the slavery worse. God renews his promise to redeem his people.

structure.title: The plagues on Egypt
structure.summary: In a series of escalating plagues, from the Nile turned to blood to three days of darkness, God shows his power over Egypt and its gods while Pharaoh repeatedly refuses to let Israel go. The death of the firstborn is announced.

structure.title: Passover, the exodus, and the sea
structure.summary: Israel keeps the first Passover, the firstborn of Egypt die, and Pharaoh drives the people out. God leads them by pillars of cloud and fire, divides the sea for Israel, and brings the waters back on Pharaoh's army. Moses and Miriam lead a song of praise.

structure.title: Through the wilderness to Sinai
structure.summary: In the desert the people grumble over water and food, and God provides sweet water, quail, manna, and water from the rock. Israel defeats Amalek, and Jethro counsels Moses to share the work of judging the people.

structure.title: The covenant at Sinai
structure.summary: At the mountain God offers Israel a covenant, speaks the Ten Commandments, and gives the laws of the Book of the Covenant. The people agree, the covenant is sealed with blood, and Israel's leaders see the God of Israel and eat in his presence.

structure.title: Instructions for the tabernacle
structure.summary: On the mountain God gives Moses the pattern for the tabernacle, its furniture, the priests' garments, and the ordination of Aaron and his sons, closing with the Sabbath as the sign of the covenant.

structure.title: The golden calf and the covenant renewed
structure.summary: While Moses is on the mountain the people worship a golden calf. Moses intercedes, God refuses to abandon them, reveals his goodness to Moses, proclaims his character, and renews the covenant.

structure.title: The tabernacle built and filled
structure.summary: The people give generously, and skilled workers build the tabernacle exactly as commanded. Moses sets it up, and the cloud covers it as the glory of the LORD fills the tent.

themes.title: The God who hears and remembers
themes.body: The rescue begins not with Israel's faith but with God's attention. When the Israelites groan under slavery, the text says that God heard their groaning and remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (2:24), and at the bush he tells Moses that he has seen their affliction and heard their cry (3:7). Remembering in the Bible is not recalling something forgotten; it means acting on a commitment. Exodus presents a God who is moved by the suffering of the powerless and keeps his promises across centuries.

themes.title: From slavery to service
themes.body: The same Hebrew root, avad, means to serve as a slave and to serve God in worship. Pharaoh makes Israel serve him ruthlessly; God's repeated demand is that Pharaoh let his people go so that they may serve him. Exodus is not a story of freedom as independence. It is a change of masters, from a king who crushes to a God who gives rest, law, and his own presence.

themes.title: Knowing the LORD
themes.body: The book turns on a name. At the bush God reveals himself as I AM and as the LORD (the divine name, usually written YHWH), and the plagues are sent so that Egypt and Israel will know that he is the LORD. Pharaoh begins by asking who the LORD is that he should obey him (5:2). By the end of the book God proclaims his own character to Moses: “compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (34:6), words the rest of the Old Testament quotes again and again.

themes.title: Covenant and law
themes.body: At Sinai God binds himself to Israel and Israel to him, calling them to be “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (19:6), a people who would show the nations what God is like. The law that follows covers worship, family, property, justice for the poor and the stranger, and the rhythm of Sabbath. It is given after the rescue, as the shape of life for people who belong to a holy God, and it assumes that failure will need forgiveness.

themes.title: God dwelling among his people
themes.body: The book's last third is about a tent. God's goal is not only to bring Israel out of Egypt but to bring them to himself and live among them. The golden calf nearly ends that hope, and Moses pleads that if God's presence does not go with them there is no point in going on (33:15). The book ends with the answer: “the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (40:34). The holiness that makes God dangerous and the mercy that makes him near are held together in that tent.

keyChapters.why: God appears in the burning bush, hears the cry of his people, sends Moses, and reveals his name, I AM WHO I AM.
The first Passover: the lamb, the blood on the doorframes, the death of Egypt's firstborn, and the night Israel goes free.
God divides the sea for Israel and destroys Pharaoh's army, the Old Testament's defining act of salvation.
At Sinai God offers the covenant and calls Israel to be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, then descends on the mountain in fire.
The Ten Commandments, grounded in the words that open them: the LORD who brought Israel out of the house of slavery.
The golden calf, Israel's first great breach of the covenant, and Moses' intercession for the people.
God proclaims his name and character to Moses and renews the broken covenant, a passage quoted throughout the Old Testament.
The tabernacle is set up and the glory of the LORD fills it, the goal toward which the whole book moves.
